readNotes: Pilot batch 1 (Nov 4 2026). Full text read first. Ledger reuse allowed for reader items (Brandon, Nov 4 3:58 PM). Distractors from chapters 0-3 only.

s1.text: When Siddhartha left the grove, where the Buddha, the perfected one, stayed behind, where Govinda stayed behind, then he felt that in this grove his past life also stayed behind and parted from him. He pondered about this sensation, which filled him completely, as he was slowly walking along. He pondered deeply, like diving into a deep water he let himself sink down to the ground of the sensation, down to the place where the causes lie, because to identify the causes, so it seemed to him, is the very essence of thinking, and by this alone sensations turn into realizations and are not lost, but become entities and start to emit like rays of light what is inside of them.

s2.text: Slowly walking along, Siddhartha pondered. He realized that he was no youth any more, but had turned into a man. He realized that one thing had left him, as a snake is left by its old skin, that one thing no longer existed in him, which had accompanied him throughout his youth and used to be a part of him: the wish to have teachers and to listen to teachings. He had also left the last teacher who had appeared on his path, even him, the highest and wisest teacher, the most holy one, Buddha, he had left him, had to part with him, was not able to accept his teachings.

s3.text: Having been pondering while slowly walking along, he now stopped as these thoughts caught hold of him, and right away another thought sprang forth from these, a new thought, which was: "That I know nothing about myself, that Siddhartha has remained thus alien and unknown to me, stems from one cause, a single cause: I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself! I searched Atman, I searched Brahman, I was willing to dissect my self and peel off all of its layers, to find the core of all peels in its unknown interior, the Atman, life, the divine part, the ultimate part. But I have lost myself in the process."

s4.text: "Oh," he thought, taking a deep breath, "now I would not let Siddhartha escape from me again! No longer, I want to begin my thoughts and my life with Atman and with the suffering of the world. I do not want to kill and dissect myself any longer, to find a secret behind the ruins. Neither Yoga-Veda shall teach me any more, nor Atharva-Veda, nor the ascetics, nor any kind of teachings. I want to learn from myself, want to be my student, want to get to know myself, the secret of Siddhartha."

s5.text: He looked around, as if he was seeing the world for the first time. Beautiful was the world, colourful was the world, strange and mysterious was the world! Here was blue, here was yellow, here was green, the sky and the river flowed, the forest and the mountains were rigid, all of it was beautiful, all of it was mysterious and magical, and in its midst was he, Siddhartha, the awakening one, on the path to himself.

s6.text: Blue was blue, river was river, and if also in the blue and the river, in Siddhartha, the singular and divine lived hidden, so it was still that very divinity's way and purpose, to be here yellow, here blue, there sky, there forest, and here Siddhartha. The purpose and the essential properties were not somewhere behind the things, they were in them, in everything.

s7.text: "How deaf and stupid have I been!" he thought, walking swiftly along. "When someone reads a text, wants to discover its meaning, he will not scorn the symbols and letters and call them deceptions, coincidence, and worthless hull, but he will read them, he will study and love them, letter by letter. But I, who wanted to read the book of the world and the book of my own being, I have, for the sake of a meaning I had anticipated before I read, scorned the symbols and letters, I called the visible world a deception, called my eyes and my tongue coincidental and worthless forms without substance. No, this is over, I have awakened, I have indeed awakened and have not been born before this very day."

s8.text: Motionless, Siddhartha remained standing there, and for the time of one moment and breath, his heart felt cold, he felt a cold in his chest, as a small animal, a bird or a rabbit, would when seeing how alone he was. For many years, he had been without home and had felt nothing. Now, he felt it. Still, even in the deepest meditation, he had been his father's son, had been a Brahmin, of a high caste, a cleric. Now, he was nothing but Siddhartha, the awoken one, nothing else was left. Deeply, he inhaled, and for a moment, he felt cold and shivered.

s9.text: Nobody was thus alone as he was. There was no nobleman who did not belong to the noblemen, no worker that did not belong to the workers, and found refuge with them, shared their life, spoke their language. No Brahmin who would not be regarded as Brahmins and lived with them, no ascetic who would not find his refuge in the caste of the Samanas, and even the most forlorn hermit in the forest was not just one and alone, he was also surrounded by a place he belonged to, he also belonged to a caste, in which he was at home. Govinda had become a monk, and a thousand monks were his brothers, wore the same robe as he, believed in his faith, spoke his language. But he, Siddhartha, where did he belong to? With whom would he share his life? Whose language would he speak?

s10.text: Out of this moment, when the world melted away all around him, when he stood alone like a star in the sky, out of this moment of a cold and despair, Siddhartha emerged, more a self than before, more firmly concentrated. He felt: This had been the last tremor of the awakening, the last struggle of this birth. And it was not long until he walked again in long strides, started to proceed swiftly and impatiently, heading no longer for home, no longer to his father, no longer back.

s11.text: But now, only in this moment, when he stopped as if a snake was lying on his path, he also awoke to this realization: "But I am no longer the one I was, I am no ascetic any more, I am not a priest any more, I am no Brahmin any more. Whatever should I do at home and at my father's place? Study? Make offerings? Practise meditation? But all this is over, all of this is no longer alongside my path."

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha decides to study the Yoga-Veda and the Atharva-Veda more carefully than ever before.
Siddhartha resolves to learn from himself instead of from teachings.
Siddhartha wishes to escape from himself for good.
Siddhartha plans to find a new teacher among the ascetics.
A.explanation: He says "I want to learn from myself, want to be my student," turning away from teachings. He says neither Veda "shall teach me any more," so studying the Vedas more carefully reverses him. He rejects "the ascetics" too. He now refuses to "let Siddhartha escape from me again," the opposite of escaping himself.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what had left Siddhartha?
options: His love of the river and the green forest
His friend Govinda and all his memories of the grove there
His old fear of the Samanas in the forest
The wish to have teachers and to listen to teachings
A.explanation: The passage names it directly: "the wish to have teachers and to listen to teachings." Govinda stayed behind, but the passage says "one thing" had left him, the wish for teachers. The river and forest are not mentioned here. Fear of the Samanas is never raised.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "shivered" most nearly means
options: stood still
sweated
trembled
sang
A.explanation: He "felt cold and shivered," so the word means trembled from cold. Singing is not suggested. Sweating is the opposite of feeling cold. "Stood still" repeats "motionless" from earlier, but shivering is a movement of the body, not stillness, so it cannot fit.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now realizes he
options: cannot simply return to his old life at home
will be welcomed home and honoured as a great Samana
must go back to the Samanas in the forest
has forgotten how to meditate properly
A.explanation: He wonders what he would do at home and decides "all of this is no longer alongside my path," so he cannot simply go back. Nothing suggests a welcome. He says "I am no ascetic any more," so returning to the Samanas is wrong. He has not forgotten meditation; he no longer wants it as his path.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Siddhartha name as the single cause of his not knowing himself?
options: He had trusted his friend Govinda far too much.
He had lived too long among the Brahmins at home.
He was afraid of himself and fled from himself.
He had never studied the holy books.
A.explanation: He says it "stems from one cause, a single cause: I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself!" Years at home are not named as the cause. He studied the books deeply in earlier chapters. Govinda is not mentioned in the passage.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "he now stopped as these thoughts caught hold of him"
"But I have lost myself in the process."
"I searched Atman, I searched Brahman"
"I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself!"
A.explanation: Only "I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself" states the single cause. The search for Atman and Brahman describes what he did, not why. "He now stopped" describes his action. "I have lost myself in the process" states the result rather than the cause.

A.prompt: The list of the nobleman, the worker, the Brahmin, the ascetic and the hermit mainly serves to
options: show that everyone else belongs somewhere, unlike Siddhartha
describe the people he meets as he walks on toward the town
rank the castes from the highest to the lowest
name the teachers Siddhartha has left behind
A.explanation: Each person "belonged" to a group and "found refuge" there, which sets off Siddhartha, who belongs nowhere. These are types, not people he meets on the road. No ranking is made. They are not named teachers; the point is belonging, not teaching.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha studies the flowing river to learn its secret.
Siddhartha sees the colourful world as beautiful, as if for the first time.
Siddhartha finds the whole world dull and grey after leaving the grove behind him.
Siddhartha decides the world is only an illusion of the senses.
A.explanation: He looks around "as if he was seeing the world for the first time" and finds it beautiful and colourful. "Dull and grey" contradicts "colourful was the world." Studying the river is not described here. The passage moves away from calling the world illusion; it is "beautiful" and "magical."

A.prompt: According to the passage, where was Siddhartha heading at the end?
options: To the forest to rejoin the Samanas there
Back to the grove to become a monk
No longer home, no longer to his father
To the river to bathe and pray
A.explanation: The passage ends: "heading no longer for home, no longer to his father, no longer back." Returning to the grove is "back," which he rejects. The Samanas are not his goal. The river and prayer are not mentioned in this passage.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "accompanied" most nearly means
options: stayed with
paid for
taught
followed angrily
A.explanation: The wish "had accompanied him throughout his youth and used to be a part of him," so it stayed with him. "Followed angrily" adds hostility the passage lacks. "Paid for" has no connection to a wish. "Taught" is wrong; the wish was for teachers, but it did not itself teach him.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now believes
options: that he has not yet awakened at all
the visible world deserves careful attention, not scorn
that reading books is a waste of time for any seeker
that his eyes and tongue are worthless forms
A.explanation: He compares the world to a text whose letters should be read and loved, and regrets having "scorned the symbols and letters," so he now values the visible world. He praises careful reading. Calling eyes and tongue worthless is his old view. He says "I have awakened."

A.prompt: The comparison "as a snake is left by its old skin" suggests that the wish for teachers
options: was poisonous and had long harmed him
still clung to him tightly
was torn from him by the Buddha
fell away naturally as he grew
A.explanation: A snake sheds its old skin as it grows, so the wish fell away naturally. The image is of shedding, not poison. He left the Buddha himself; nothing was torn from him. The comparison says the wish "no longer existed in him," so it did not cling.

B.prompt: According to the passage, what did it seem to Siddhartha was the very essence of thinking?
options: Listening to a teacher
Identifying the causes
Walking slowly along the road
Remembering the holy verses
B.explanation: The passage says "to identify the causes, so it seemed to him, is the very essence of thinking." Remembering verses is not mentioned. He walks slowly, but walking is not called thinking's essence. He has just left all teachers, so listening to one is wrong.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "scorn" most nearly means
options: look down on
study with love
misread
forget
B.explanation: A reader "will not scorn the symbols and letters and call them deceptions," so to scorn is to look down on. Studying with love is what the passage contrasts with scorn. "Misread" and "forget" describe errors, but the passage is about contempt for the letters.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that, until this moment, Siddhartha's caste had
options: made him feel lonely and cold among the other Brahmins
kept him from meditating each day
been unknown to him
given him a sense of belonging even in meditation
B.explanation: Even "in the deepest meditation, he had been his father's son, had been a Brahmin," and only "Now" he feels alone, so his caste gave belonging. He says he "had felt nothing" before, not loneliness. It did not stop meditation. He clearly knew his caste.

B.prompt: Based on the passage, what mistake does Siddhartha say he made?
options: He scorned the visible world for a meaning he had decided on in advance.
He read too many books and spent too little time looking at the world.
He forgot to study every letter of the holy books carefully and slowly.
He trusted his eyes and tongue too much.
B.explanation: He says that "for the sake of a meaning I had anticipated before I read," he "scorned the symbols and letters." Too much reading is not his complaint. He called his eyes and tongue "worthless," the opposite of trusting them. His mistake was scorn of the world, not forgetting the holy books.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "I have, for the sake of a meaning I had anticipated before I read, scorned the symbols and letters"
"When someone reads a text, wants to discover its meaning, he will not scorn the symbols and letters"
"How deaf and stupid have I been!"
"I have indeed awakened and have not been born before this very day."
B.explanation: Only the line about the meaning "anticipated before I read" names his mistake. The "When someone reads a text" line describes a good reader, not his error. "How deaf and stupid" shows regret but not what the mistake was. "I have indeed awakened" describes his new state.

B.prompt: The list "Neither Yoga-Veda... nor Atharva-Veda, nor the ascetics, nor any kind of teachings" mainly serves to
options: name the books he plans to read when he reaches town
praise the ascetics far above the Vedas
reject every outside source of teaching at once
show that he has forgotten the Vedas
B.explanation: Each "nor" adds another source, ending with "any kind of teachings," so all outside teaching is rejected. He plans to read none of them. The ascetics are rejected along with the Vedas, not praised. Naming the Vedas shows he remembers them.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha runs quickly from the grove without stopping to think.
Siddhartha senses his past life left behind and thinks deeply about this feeling.
Siddhartha weeps as he walks away, longing to go back to the grove.
Siddhartha explains the teachings of the Buddha.
B.explanation: He feels his "past life also stayed behind" and ponders the sensation deeply. No weeping or longing to return is described. He walks "slowly" and thinks, the opposite of running without thought. He does not explain the Buddha's teachings here.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "tremor" most nearly means
options: step forward
loud noise
fear of the dark
shudder
B.explanation: This "had been the last tremor of the awakening," following his shivering, so it means a shudder. A loud noise is not described. "Fear of the dark" narrows it wrongly. "Step forward" is what follows the tremor, not what the word means.

B.prompt: The questions at the end of the passage mainly serve to
options: show that Siddhartha has found a new home
ask Govinda where he will live now as a monk
introduce a new character to the story
stress how completely alone Siddhartha feels
B.explanation: "Where did he belong to? With whom would he share his life?" have no answers, stressing his isolation. Govinda is not being asked anything; these are Siddhartha's own thoughts. No new character appears. The questions show he has no home.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now believes the divine
options: can only be found by ignoring the visible world
lives only in the Brahmins and their rites
is found within things, not hidden behind them
has left the world
B.explanation: "The purpose and the essential properties were not somewhere behind the things, they were in them, in everything." Ignoring the visible world is his old view. The divine is "in everything," not only in Brahmins. It is present "here yellow, here blue," so it has not left.

B.prompt: The passage is presented mainly as
options: a teaching given by the Buddha
a conversation between Siddhartha and Govinda on the road
Siddhartha's own words as he examines himself
the narrator's summary of the Vedas
B.explanation: Most of the passage is quoted thought ("I was afraid of myself"), so it is self-examination in his own words. Govinda is not present. The Buddha does not speak. The Vedas are not summarized; Atman and Brahman are named only as what he searched for.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 extend the change described in Passage 1?
options: It shows Siddhartha sadly missing his old teachers.
It shows that leaving teachers also means he cannot return home.
It shows Siddhartha deciding to go back and become a monk.
It shows that nothing has really changed.
B.explanation: Passage 1 says he no longer wants teachers; Passage 2 says "I am no ascetic any more... no Brahmin any more," so home is closed too. He does not return to the Buddha. He does not miss teachers. Both passages describe real change.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: The workers and noblemen are at war with each other.
Siddhartha finds a hermit as lonely as he is and joins him.
Unlike everyone else, Siddhartha belongs to no group.
Govinda feels alone among the monks.
C.explanation: Everyone, "even the most forlorn hermit," belongs to "a caste," while Siddhartha asks "where did he belong to?" The hermit is "not just one and alone," so the choice about joining a lonely hermit is wrong. Govinda has "a thousand monks" as brothers. No war is mentioned.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's search for Atman was in part
options: a way of running from himself
a game he played for fun
a plan suggested by Govinda
a great success that taught him everything
C.explanation: He searched Atman and Brahman, then concludes "I was fleeing from myself" and "I have lost myself in the process," so the search was partly flight. It did not teach him about himself; he knows "nothing about myself." Govinda is not mentioned. Nothing suggests it was a game.

C.prompt: The sentence "Here was blue, here was yellow, here was green" mainly serves to
options: list the colours of the monks' robes in the grove
describe a painting
show that Siddhartha is confused and dizzy
convey the freshness of simple sensory experience
C.explanation: Short, plain statements of colour convey a fresh, direct seeing. The monks wear yellow, but the sentence names many colours in nature. He is "the awakening one," not confused. No painting is described; he sees the sky, river and forest.

C.prompt: Based on the passage, what is the result of Siddhartha's moment of despair?
options: He falls asleep by the side of the road.
He forgets who he is.
He becomes more himself and more focused.
He gives up his search and returns to his father.
C.explanation: Out of the moment of cold and despair, "Siddhartha emerged, more a self than before, more firmly concentrated." He heads "no longer to his father." He walks on "in long strides," not to sleep. He becomes more himself, not less.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "This had been the last tremor of the awakening, the last struggle of this birth."
"Siddhartha emerged, more a self than before, more firmly concentrated."
"Out of this moment, when the world melted away all around him, when he stood alone like a star in the sky"
"heading no longer for home, no longer to his father, no longer back."
C.explanation: Only "more a self than before, more firmly concentrated" states the result. "When the world melted away" describes the moment itself. "The last tremor" names what the moment was. "Heading no longer for home" shows direction, not the inner change.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "coincidental" most nearly means
options: timed by careful planning
sacred
beautiful
accidental
C.explanation: Siddhartha says he "called my eyes and my tongue coincidental and worthless forms without substance," so the sense is accidental, without purpose or meaning. "Timed by careful planning" mixes another meaning with its opposite. "Beautiful" and "sacred" describe how he now values the world, not what "coincidental" means.

C.prompt: The comparison of the world to a text with letters mainly suggests that
options: the visible world should be read closely, not dismissed
the holy books matter more than anything in the visible world
Siddhartha has finally learned to write
letters and words are only deceptions
C.explanation: A good reader studies and loves the letters "letter by letter"; Siddhartha regrets scorning the world's "symbols and letters," so the world should be read closely. He does not say books outrank the world. Writing is not discussed. Calling letters deceptions is exactly what a good reader will not do.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that, for Siddhartha, thinking matters because it
options: pleases his teachers and his father
turns passing feelings into lasting understanding
helps him forget everything that happened in the grove
makes him feel sad
C.explanation: By identifying causes, "sensations turn into realizations and are not lost," so thinking turns feelings into lasting understanding. He is not trying to forget; he ponders his past. He has left his teachers. Sadness is not named as its effect.

C.prompt: The contrast "For many years... had felt nothing. Now, he felt it" mainly serves to
options: explain why he left home years ago
compare Siddhartha with his friend Govinda
show that he has been ill for years and is now healing
mark a sudden change in what Siddhartha feels
C.explanation: The two short statements set years of feeling nothing against "Now, he felt it," marking sudden change. Illness is not mentioned. Govinda is not compared here. Leaving home happened long ago in the first chapter and is not explained by this contrast.

C.prompt: The short statements "Blue was blue, river was river" mainly present Siddhartha's new view as
options: plain and certain acceptance of things as they are
a joke made at the Brahmins' expense
a mistake he will soon regret
a riddle no reader can solve without a teacher
C.explanation: Plain statements of identity show calm, certain acceptance of things as they are. They are simple, not a riddle needing a teacher. Nothing mocks the Brahmins here. The passage presents the view approvingly, and no later regret is hinted at anywhere.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 relate to the resolution in Passage 1?
options: It describes a new teacher he plans to follow.
It explains why he now wants to learn from himself and the world.
It repeats the resolution word for word.
It shows that he regrets his resolution and wishes to return to the Vedas.
C.explanation: Passage 1 resolves to learn from himself; Passage 2 explains his past mistake of scorning the visible world, giving the reason. He does not regret the resolution. No teacher is described. The wording differs; Passage 2 develops rather than repeats.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 develop the moment described in Passage 1?
options: It shows that the moment never really ends.
It shows him falling ill from the cold night air.
It shows the cold loneliness turning into new strength.
It shows Siddhartha giving in to fear and running back.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows him cold and alone; Passage 2 says he "emerged, more a self than before." He heads "no longer back," so he does not run to the grove. No illness follows. Passage 2 calls it "the last tremor," so the moment ends.
